title: The founder film
scenario:
Northgate Bakery sends two long files for its brand library. You plan how to read them. For video you use a Gemini model with a 1M context window. For the interview you use OpenAI transcription.

The file list and the notes in the exhibit are made up for this case.
exhibit:
Files (made up)
  founder-interview.mp3   90 minutes, 86 MB
  brand-film.mp4          130 minutes

Needs
  The small print on the flour sacks in the film must be readable, so
  fine detail matters.

Notes from a first test (made up)
  Film: a fast whip-pan to the new loaf, about 2 seconds long, near 12:05.
        The model's description of the film skips it.
  Interview: the finished transcript is about 70,000 tokens.
  Model answer: "The oven door scene is at 41:20."

questions.prompt: What do you do with the 86 MB interview for OpenAI transcription?

options.text: Send the 86 MB file as it is. The API will split it into the right sizes by itself, for you.
options.explanation: OpenAI's transcription API accepts files up to 25 MB. A larger file has to be compressed or split first.

options.text: Convert it to uncompressed WAV so the audio is as clean as possible before it is sent.
options.explanation: WAV is larger, not smaller. OpenAI says to use a compressed format or to split the file.

options.text: Split it into 25 MB chunks or less, cutting at pauses between speakers, not mid-sentence.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI says to split into chunks of 25 MB or less and to avoid splitting in the middle of a sentence.

options.text: Cut it into exact 25 MB pieces with no gaps, so that no audio is lost at any of the joins.
options.explanation: OpenAI warns that splitting in the middle of a sentence can remove context and reduce accuracy.

questions.prompt: How do you read the 130-minute film when the small print must be readable?

options.text: Send all 130 minutes in one request at high media resolution. The limit is 3 hours.
options.explanation: The 3-hour limit is for low media resolution. At high resolution Google lists up to 1 hour.

options.text: Send it in one request at low media resolution. 130 minutes is under 3 hours, so detail is no problem.
options.explanation: Low resolution fits the length, but the brief needs readable small print. Detail and length trade against each other.

options.text: Set fps to 10 for the whole film, so that more frames reach the model in a single request.
options.explanation: More frames do not raise the length limit. They add more to read in one request.

options.text: Split the film into parts shorter than one hour, and send each part at high media resolution.
options.explanation: Right. Google lists up to 1 hour at high media resolution for models with a 1M window. Three parts of about 43 minutes fit.

questions.prompt: The whip-pan to the new loaf is missing from the description. What is the best fix?

options.text: Re-run only that stretch of the film, clipped with start and end offsets, at a higher fps.
options.explanation: Right. Google says 1 frame per second may miss rapid motion. In static mode, it lets you set fps and clip a video.

options.text: Lower fps to 0.5 for the whole film, so the model has fewer frames to look at carefully.
options.explanation: A lower rate reads even fewer frames, so a 2-second shot is even more likely to be missed.

options.text: Ask the model to try harder. It already reads every frame of the film by default.
options.explanation: The default is 1 frame per second, not every frame. A fast shot can fall between samples.

options.text: Accept the gap. The sampling rate cannot be changed, so a fast shot is always lost.
options.explanation: Google documents an fps setting, so the rate can be changed.

questions.prompt: How do you lay out the prompt for the 70,000-token transcript with a Claude model?

options.text: Put the question first and the transcript after it, so the model knows the goal before it reads.
options.explanation: Anthropic says to put longform data at the top, above the question and the instructions.

options.text: Put the transcript at the top, then the question, and ask for the relevant quotes before the answer.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic advises longform data at the top and asking the model to quote relevant parts first.

options.text: Cut it into ten parts and ask the same question in ten separate chats, then join the answers.
options.explanation: Each chat sees only a tenth of the interview. Anything that links two parts is lost.

options.text: Write a three-line summary yourself and send only that, with the question, to save tokens.
options.explanation: A summary hides the exact words, so the model cannot quote the lines that matter.

questions.prompt: The model says the oven door scene is at 41:20. What do you do before it goes into the library?

options.text: Use 41:20 as it is. MM:SS is the format Google documents, so the time must be exact.
options.explanation: A documented format does not make the time correct. A model that samples video can be off.

options.text: Ask the model for the time again. If it gives 41:20 twice, the answer is confirmed.
options.explanation: The same answer twice is not a check. Only the file itself can confirm the moment.

options.text: Round every time to the nearest minute, so that small errors cannot matter.
options.explanation: Rounding makes the pointer less useful. Nobody can find a 5-second shot from a minute.

options.text: Open the file at 41:20, check the scene, then add the checked row to the moment sheet.
options.explanation: Right. This is our habit: a timestamp is a pointer until a person has opened the file there.
